claims.text: Surface segregation governs the onset of premelting and melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Selected species can segregate to the surface of a high-entropy alloy.
The segregating surface species are lower-melting-point species.
Surface enrichment by lower-melting-point species creates local strain fields.
A segregated surface has a lower effective melting point than a uniform, randomly mixed surface.
Bottom-up synthesis can produce nearly homogeneous, randomly mixed multi-element nanoparticles in the approximately 2–20 nm size range.
Controlled post-synthesis annealing or selective surface treatment can induce segregation of lower-melting-point species while leaving bulk composition unchanged.
An inert atmosphere prevents oxidation during thermal testing.
Localized strain fields weaken interatomic bonds at the nanoparticle surface.
Weakened surface bonds cause an earlier onset of premelting.
Weakened surface bonds reduce the effective melting temperature of the nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with induced surface segregation will premelt and melt at lower temperatures than nanoparticles with a uniform surface composition.
The proposed segregation effect holds for nanoparticles between 2 and 20 nm under an inert atmosphere.
Minor compositional variations and interparticle interactions may influence the magnitude of the melting-temperature shift.
In situ TEM and DSC can be used to compare premelting and melting onset temperatures between treated and baseline nanoparticles.
EDS mapping can confirm a difference in surface composition between treated and baseline nanoparticles.
